entries.text:
The ozone layer is healing
After the Montreal Protocol was signed in September 1987, clear signs have emerged that the ozone layer is beginning to recover. The UN-backed Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion, published in October 2026, projects the near-global average back at 1980 values around 2040, and the Antarctic during the 2060s, provided countries keep complying with the treaty.
A global treaty, strengthened by amendments over time.

claims.claim: The Montreal Protocol was adopted in September 1987

sources.quote: Conference, on 16 September 1987, adopted the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer

claims.claim: Clear signs show the ozone layer is beginning to recover

sources.quote: clear signs that the stratospheric ozone layer is beginning to recover have emerged

claims.claim: Near-global ozone is projected back at 1980 values around 2040; Antarctic during the 2060s; provided continued compliance; published October 2026

sources.quote: Antarctic TCO is projected to return to 1980 values during the 2060s ... Near-global-mean TCO is projected to return to 1980 values around 2040 ... provided there is continued compliance. (Published October 2026)

claims.claim: The assessment is UN-backed (WMO and UNEP)

sources.quote: World Meteorological Organization ... United Nations Environment Programme (publishers of the Assessment)

claims.claim: The treaty has been strengthened by amendments over time

sources.quote: 1990 London Adjustment and Amendment ... 1992 Copenhagen Adjustment and Amendment ... 2016 Kigali Amendment

entries.notes: Replaced the 2022-assessment figures (Arctic 2045, Antarctic ~2066, "nearly 99 per cent" phase-out) with the October 2026 assessment, which now says Antarctic during the 2060s and does not give an Arctic date or the 99% figure. Source switched from UN News (2023) to the assessment itself.

entries.text:
Humpback whales are recovering
Most humpback whale stocks have been recovering from whaling since the International Whaling Commission’s moratorium on commercial whaling took effect in the mid-1980s, and the species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Some small subpopulations, such as the one in Oceania, are still listed as Endangered.
An international hunting ban that countries kept.

claims.claim: Most humpback stocks are recovering since the commercial-whaling moratorium took effect in the mid-1980s

sources.quote: Further protection for the species came into force in 1986 with the Moratorium established by the IWC ... An overall recovery of about 70% for all stocks combined is indicated
in effect since 1985, played a major role in the recovery of humpback whales

claims.claim: The species is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List

sources.quote: has moved from Vulnerable to Least Concern, meaning it is at low risk of extinction
is currently listed as “Least Concern” on the IUCN Red List

claims.claim: Some small subpopulations, such as Oceania, are still listed as Endangered

sources.quote: Two subpopulations still have Endangered status
low numbers of the Oceania stocks have meant these are still listed as “Endangered”

claims.claim: The recovery is credited to protection from commercial hunting

sources.quote: are making a comeback in much of their range mainly because they have been protected from commercial hunting

entries.notes: "1986" changed to "the mid-1980s" (Frontiers says 1986, NOAA says 1985). "A few small stocks" changed to "Some small subpopulations": IUCN says two subpopulations; only Oceania is named by a current source. Added the IUCN press release as a primary source.

entries.text:
The Iberian lynx pulled back from the brink
In June 2024 the IUCN moved the Iberian lynx from Endangered to Vulnerable: mature individuals grew from 62 in 2001 to 648 in 2022, and the total population is now estimated at over 2,000.
More rabbits to eat, protected and rebuilt scrub and forest, fewer human-caused deaths, and breeding and reintroduction (over 400 lynx released since 2010).

claims.claim: In June 2024 the IUCN moved the Iberian lynx from Endangered to Vulnerable

sources.quote: has improved from Endangered to Vulnerable (20 June 2024)

sources.quote: increasing exponentially from 62 mature individuals in 2001 to 648 in 2022 ... estimated to be more than 2,000

claims.claim: Causes: more rabbits, protected and restored scrub and forest, fewer human-caused deaths, breeding and reintroduction (400+ since 2010)

sources.quote: increasing the abundance of its prey ... protecting and restoring Mediterranean scrub and forest habitat ... reducing deaths caused by human activity ... more than 400 Iberian lynx have been reintroduced

entries.notes: Text unchanged. Source switched from Euronews to the IUCN press release (primary).

entries.text:
Giant pandas are no longer Endangered
In 2016 the IUCN moved the giant panda from Endangered to Vulnerable, as surveys showed the wild population had started to increase.
A crackdown on poaching, and protecting and restoring panda habitat.

claims.claim: Surveys showed the wild population had started to increase

sources.quote: the previous population decline has been arrested, and the population has started to increase

claims.claim: Credited to a crackdown on poaching and protecting/restoring habitat

sources.quote: the hard work of controlling poaching and replanting bamboo forests
A marked decrease in poaching ... and a huge expansion of the animal's protected habitat
crackdown on poaching and the restoration of the pandas' habitat

entries.notes: Dropped "the IUCN said the decline had been arrested" (only one source opened; kept to what several sources show). Cause reworded to what all three sources support (poaching crackdown, protected and restored habitat).

entries.text:
The saiga antelope is recovering
On 11 December 2023 the IUCN moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened. Kazakhstan’s population rose from under 50,000 in 2005 to over 1.9 million.
Anti-poaching measures, stronger law enforcement and border control, and major new state protected areas.

claims.claim: On 11 December 2023 the IUCN moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened

sources.quote: Saiga Antelope Moves from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened Category on IUCN Red List (12 December 2023)
The published saiga assessment on the Red List website can be found here from the afternoon of 11th December

claims.claim: Kazakhstan's population rose from under 50,000 in 2005 to over 1.9 million

sources.quote: recovered from a perilously low estimate of 48,000 in 2005 to now over 1.9 million
recovered from a perilously low estimate of just 39,000 in 2005 to now over 1.9 million

claims.claim: Recovery credited to anti-poaching, law enforcement and border control, and new state protected areas

sources.quote: anti-poaching initiatives, robust law enforcement and border control measures, and establishment of a series of major new State Protected Areas
anti-poaching initiatives, robust law enforcement and border control measures, and establishment of a series of major new State Protected Areas

entries.notes: The 2005 baseline is 48,000 in Astana Times but 39,000 in the WCS release; both are under 50,000, so the card now says "under 50,000". "Population monitoring and community-led ranger teams" came from one source only and was dropped from the cause line. Down To Earth replaced by Astana Times + WCS.

entries.text:
The bald eagle came back from DDT
Bald eagles in the lower 48 states fell to an all-time low of 417 breeding pairs in 1963, mainly because the pesticide DDT weakened their eggshells. By 2007 there were 9,789 pairs, and the Interior Department announced the bird’s removal from the endangered species list.
Ending the DDT threat and legal protection for the birds.

entries.text: The Global Carbon Budget 2025 projected 38.1 billion tonnes of fossil CO2 emissions for 2025, about 1% more than in 2024 and a record high. It put the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5°C at 170 billion tonnes of CO2, nearly exhausted: around four years at 2025 emission levels.

entries.text: MAAP, a research programme of Amazon Conservation, estimates that 15% of the Amazon biome’s original primary forest had been lost by the end of 2025. A 2018 paper by Nobre and Lovejoy warned that the forest could tip toward savanna at 20–25% deforestation, a threshold that is debated.

entries.text:
Goal: survive the turns shown. Keep the ecosystem bar above the red line and keep every species alive.
Each turn you get ⚡ Energy to spend on actions. Unspent Energy is lost.
Tiles are Healthy, Damaged or Lost. Each threat hit moves a tile down one step.
Red arrows show exactly where every threat will strike when you end your turn. Nothing is hidden.
Each species needs a number of Healthy tiles of its habitat. With fewer, it loses a ♥ every turn. At 0 ♥ it is gone.
Actions: Restore 1⚡ · Defend 1⚡ · Remove 2⚡ · Protect 3⚡ · Campaign 3⚡.
Tiles marked ⚠ are risky for activists: acting there costs +1⚡.
Stars: ★ survive · ★★ finish at least as healthy as you started · ★★★ every threat stopped.
entries.notes: The rulebook describes how the game works. It makes no statement about the real world.
